title: A Shark Graveyard Hidden in Egypt's Desert
summary:
Picture a scorching desert in Egypt. Now picture it underwater, swarming with sharks. That's exactly what scientists say this area looked like 70 to 80 million years ago.

A team of paleontologists led by Dr. Tarek Yassin of Cairo University discovered what they're calling a "shark graveyard" in Egypt's Western Desert. Their findings, published in the journal Cretaceous Research on August 18, 2026, describe 14 fossilized shark teeth found in dark, phosphate-rich rocks on the Abu-Tartur Plateau.

The teeth came in a surprising variety of shapes. Some were slender and needle-like, built for grasping slippery prey. Others were wider with serrated edges, designed for slicing. The teeth belonged to five different shark species, two of which had never been found in Egypt before.

One of the most exciting finds was an ancient relative of today's goblin shark, a deep-sea species that still exists. This may be the first time it has been found in Africa, and possibly the youngest known example of the shark. The team also identified an extinct crow shark.

So how did so many teeth end up in one spot? Not from a single disaster. Over millions of years, generations of sharks shed their teeth on the seafloor. The teeth were buried in sediment, which eventually hardened into rock. Because the teeth built up over such a long time, the different species may never have lived there at the same time.

"What makes this discovery especially significant is that it gives us a glimpse into a much more diverse marine ecosystem than we previously knew existed in this part of North Africa," Dr. Yassin said. He added that this is likely only one piece of a much larger story, and the team hopes to keep exploring.

This discovery reminds us that landscapes can change dramatically over millions of years. A sea can become a desert, and its ancient residents can be preserved in stone, waiting for scientists to find them.
why_it_matters: Findings like this show how scientists reconstruct whole ecosystems from small clues, and they underline that today's climate and geography are temporary — the same land can be seabed, then desert, with the record of both locked in the rock beneath us.

background_read: During the Cretaceous period — the final chapter of the age of dinosaurs, which ended about 66 million years ago — a shallow sea called the Tethys covered large parts of what is now North Africa, including areas of modern Egypt. That is why marine fossils, from shells to shark teeth, turn up in places that are bone-dry desert today.

Sharks are ideal fossils for this kind of study because they never stop shedding teeth: a single shark can lose thousands over its lifetime, and tooth material is hard enough to survive burial far better than soft body parts. The teeth found here were preserved in sediment that later hardened into rock, so what geologists now mine as phosphate deposits also traps traces of ancient sea life.

The goblin shark (Mitsukurina owstoni) is a rare deep-sea species often described as a 'living fossil', because its family has survived for tens of millions of years while most of its relatives disappeared. Finding an ancient relative in Africa would extend what scientists know about where this lineage lived.

Cairo University, founded in the early twentieth century, is one of Egypt's oldest and largest universities, and its researchers frequently work on fossils and geology in the Western Desert, where phosphate is mined for fertilizer.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — new records for African prehistory
perspectives.description: Two shark species never before found in Egypt, plus a possible first African record of a goblin-shark relative, expand the map of where these animals lived. The site suggests North Africa hosted a richer marine ecosystem than scientists had assumed.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — 14 teeth is a thin sample
perspectives.description: Fourteen teeth from five species is a small dataset, and shark species are often identified mainly by tooth shape, which can be ambiguous across related species. Some researchers would want more material before treating the goblin-shark identification as settled.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — a time-averaged snapshot of an ancient sea
perspectives.description: The authors point out that the teeth accumulated over millions of years rather than in one event, which means species found together may never have met. That makes the site valuable as a record of long-term change, but complicated to read as a single living community.

Dr. Yassin describes the find as one piece of a much larger story, and the team plans to keep exploring the plateau. Further digging — and careful dating of the rock layers — could reveal whether more of this ancient sea's inhabitants are still waiting to be found.
